rv.q: Coriolanus is the first Shakespeare play Turner has directed since, and she’s clearly learned a few tricks over the last decade, because this is tremendous.
David Oyelowo makes a scorching return to the UK stage in this tightly focused, ferocious staging of Shakespeare’s Roman play.
Oyelowo, all but lost to theatre in recent years, gives a towering performance of coiled intensity, as well as notable verbal dexterity.

That fact is front and central in Lyndsey Turner’s mighty production of Coriolanus, led by a terrific, deeply troubled David Oyelowo, which fuses past and present, public space and playing space, to brilliantly eloquent effect.
In all, it’s a great yarn, thrillingly told.
Lyndsey Turner’s vaulting revival, starring David Oyelowo, thrillingly aligns the play’s tricky contours with a modern, ill-at-ease Britain.
Oyelowo’s is an immensely watchable central performance and Turner’s take on the play is intelligent, but it sacrifices some of the excitement.
What is less effective is the force of the drama itself, which is woodenly underpowered and never evokes quite enough feeling.
Yet Lyndsey Turner’s spectacular production turns his story into a portentous version of dystopian sci-fi movies The Hunger Games.
The mix of period and modern, blends remarkably effectively and the results are never less than strong and sophisticated.

It is an ending that isn’t quite the end, for there is a final image to what is a spectacular production where design, music and lighting contribute a great deal and so effectively that they sometimes take attention away from the spoken.
Even when passion is missing, Turner's production remains a glorious sight.
Nomvete’s performance is exquisite and brings the role of mother to the centre of work.
David Oyelowo plays the eponymous anti-hero with viper fangs hissing venom in all directions.
As an exemplar of the virtuous man of arms, he is possibly perfect, but as a dramatic character, not so much.
This is a flawed revival of a flawed play, but, nonetheless, much of it remains intriguing.
Yet it’s a slick production rather than an involving one.
If you feel you ought to see Coriolanus – perhaps you haven’t ticked that box yet – you’ll find this an acceptable option.

cn.t: Turner's visually stunning production features a powerful Oyelowo, but critics are divided on whether the spectacle overwhelms the drama. Praised for timely political resonance and design, yet some find it too cool and considered for Shakespeare's muscular tragedy.
